t: standing. In a standing position.
sitting in a ship or a wagon. Which are sometimes tossed about, making it hard to stand in them.
even lying on his side. But he should not pray lying on his back or on his face (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:2).
provided that he can focus his mind. For if he cannot concentrate because of his illness, he should not pray.
likewise the thirsty and the hungry are included among the sick. They must first examine whether they can concentrate in prayer.
he should not pray until he eats and drinks. So that his hunger or thirst leaves him and his mind settles (and see below, halachah 15).
if he was riding on an animal... he need not dismount. For even if another holds his animal, his mind is not settled because of the delay on the road.
he turns his face toward the Land of Israel. He faces in the direction of the Land of Israel.
standing in the Temple. Praying in the Temple itself.
the Holy of Holies. The most sacred part of the Temple, where the Ark of the Covenant was placed.
a blind person. Blind.
one who cannot determine the directions. Who does not know the compass directions.
one traveling in a ship. Who does not know where Jerusalem lies.
he should direct his heart toward the Divine Presence. He should imagine that he is standing before God.
he should place his feet side by side. Bringing them together.
and he casts his eyes downward. He turns his eyes toward the ground (see below 5:7 [14:7], Hilchot De'ot 5:8).
turned upward. Directed upward.
folded. Clasped, which is a manner of submission.
and he should not place his hands on his hips. On his loins, for this is a manner of arrogance.
he first arranges his clothing, adorns himself and beautifies himself. He straightens his clothes and dresses well.
in his apundah. A garment worn against the flesh that absorbs sweat, with no other garment over it.
nor with a bare head. For covering the head indicates fear of Heaven.
in the foot-coverings. In the covering of the feet.
because his mind is preoccupied with them. He is careful lest they fall.

he prays with the lulav in his hand during the days of the festival. For those who are scrupulous about the mitzvah of lulav were accustomed to take the four species in their hands on the way to the synagogue and to hold them throughout the prayer (see Hilchot Lulav 7:24).
if he had a load on his head... he drops it behind him. If he was carrying an object on his head, he moves it to his shoulder so that it does not disturb his prayer.
if it was four kavs. For a load of this volume disturbs prayer.
only when they are wrapped. In an outer garment (see Hilchot Tzitzit 3:11).
in a low place. Relatively low within the house (see below 5:7).
and he turns his face to the wall. He faces the wall.
and his windows were open in his upper room toward Jerusalem. Windows were open to him in his upper room facing Jerusalem, toward which Daniel prayed.
and he sets a permanent place for his prayer. He designates a place in which to pray.
in a ruin. A ruined building.
nor behind the synagogue etc.. Because it appears as disrespect for the synagogue.
and it is forbidden to sit beside one who stands in prayer etc.. Out of respect for the prayer.
four cubits. Which is the place of the one praying.
three handbreadths high or more. For up to this height it is considered a single level (see Hilchot Shabbat 14:7).

four cubits... which is the measure of a house. For many halachic purposes, since then it is considered fit for dwelling (see Hilchot Tefillin 6:1, Hilchot Eruvin 1:16, Hilchot Ishut 13:3 and others).
like an upper room. A second story, which is not considered an elevated place, because it is not measured relative to the house.
if it was surrounded by a partition... because its height is not noticeable. If that place was surrounded by partitions, so that from within it does not appear raised.
craftsmen. Tradesmen employed by another.
they come down and pray. So that they stand in a low place (compare Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:4).
because their trouble is great. For the climbing down and up these trees can take a long time, and they neglect the work of their employer.
and how do they pray. How far those tradesmen, who pray while at work, were permitted to shorten their prayer because of neglecting the employer's work.

if they were working for their meals only etc.. They receive as wages only that day's meals; since their pay is small and there is no great loss in their idleness, they pray the full prayer (see Hilchot Berakhot 2:2).
if they were working for wages, they pray the abbreviated prayer. If they receive wages beyond the day's meals, they must hurry in their work and pray an abbreviated prayer (see above 2:2-3).
they do not go down before the ark etc.. Because it involves excessive length.
he should not raise his voice. He should not pray aloud.
nor pray in his heart. By merely thinking the words.
he articulates the words with his lips. He pronounces them with his mouth in a low voice (compare Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:8).
so that he not be among the congregation etc.. Even one who is permitted to make his voice heard should not do so among a congregation, since this disturbs them.
he bows five times. In total, during the prayer, as will be explained.
and he takes leave from his left side etc.. While bowing, he turns left and then right, as in a farewell greeting (see below halachah 11, Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:4).
he bows at "Baruch". He bends his body when saying the word "Baruch."
he straightens at the Name. When he reaches the Name of God.
but the High Priest... and the king etc.. For the greater a person is, the more fitting it is for him to multiply signs of submission before God.
that is, as though he stands before the king. And as if turning to the right of the one standing opposite him.
that he take leave of the prayer. He ends the prayer and takes leave of it.
they take leave. They part.
until all the vertebrae of the spine are loosened. That the vertebrae protrude from the bowing.
he bent. He bowed himself down.
and he exerted himself and appeared as one bowing etc.. If he strained to bow and it is evident that he is capable of no more, that suffices.

and he supplicates with any supplications he wishes. For there is no fixed text for this (for the placement of supplications in the order of prayer see below 7:17-18, 9:5-8; and see also Seder HaTefillot, 33-34).
the bowing mentioned everywhere. Which is the beginning of prostration (see for example Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 2:7, Hilchot Shegagot 14:2).
on his face. Tilting the face downward.
spreading out the hands and feet. Lying with hands and feet stretched out.
after he lifts his head from the fifth bow. After he finishes the Amidah.
and falls on his face to the ground. He prostrates himself on the ground, and this is the prostration, as described below.
there are those who do etc.. There is no fixed custom in the matter.
and it is forbidden to prostrate on stones etc.. For the Torah forbade this because it was the manner of idolatrous worship.
as we explained in Hilchot Avodah Zarah. 6:6-7.
and a distinguished person is not permitted etc.. For if he is not answered, he has been disgraced by this falling for nothing.
that he is righteous like Joshua. That he will certainly be answered, like Joshua son of Nun, who fell on his face before the Ark of God and was answered in his prayer (see Joshua 7:6-10).
he inclines his face slightly. For this is not a full prostration (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 6:7).
widespread. Common.
and some individuals fall on their faces at Ma'ariv. But this is not a prevalent custom (see below 7:19).
to pass behind the synagogue etc.. So that they not suspect him of avoiding communal prayer.
unless he was carrying a load. And it is clear that he is busy, and for that reason does not enter.
on two sides. On different sides of the building.
to the synagogue he is accustomed to. Which is the second synagogue.
one who pursues mitzvot. One who is careful to fulfil the commandments.
he should not prolong his prayer excessively. Rather, he should match his prayer to the congregation's.
even like the order of the Yom Kippur confession. The confession said on Yom Kippur after the prayer (Hilchot Teshuvah 2:7-8), which is very long.
of the nature of the blessing. Additions on the same subject.
according to the eloquence of his tongue. According to his ability of expression (see above 1:3-4).
he should not ask in the first three nor in the last three. For these are not blessings of requesting needs, but of praise and thanksgiving (see also above 1:9).
that he taste anything. That he eat a small amount.
after the dawn has risen. Which is the beginning of the time of the morning prayer (above 3:7).
to his friend's door. To his friend's house.
and he should not set out on a journey before he prays. For he must pray first, before doing any of his affairs.
he does not dine close to Minchah. Lest he neglect the prayer, as below halachah 5.
the time of Minchah Gedolah. Half an hour after midday (above 3:2-4).
even to perspire. Even if he does not enter to wash, but only to sweat from the heat of the bathhouse.
lest he faint. Lest he become weak from the bathhouse vapors and the heat there.
a casual meal. A small meal.
even at the conclusion of a judgment. At the stage of the decision of the verdict and its conclusion (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 10:2, 21:3).
lest the judgment be overturned and drag on. That a reason will be found to refute the conclusion of the ruling (Hilchot Sanhedrin 7:6 and elsewhere), and they will deliberate again at length.
an ordinary haircut. Simple, not elaborate.
the scissors. The shears.
the tanner. A leather-processing workshop.
and if he began... he does not stop but finishes. This is a precaution taken out of concern, and if he has already begun, we do not worry about it (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:6).
the start of the haircut. The stage at which, if he has begun, he does not stop but finishes and prays afterward.
the barbers' cloth. A sheet of cloth spread over the body during a haircut.
once he ties it between his shoulders. He ties the ends of his garments behind him so they do not interfere with his work.
once the judges wrap themselves. They cover themselves with an outer garment, in preparation for judgment (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 3:7).
even though the evening prayer is optional. And it is treated somewhat leniently (see above 3:7), they were concerned about its neglect because Israel accepted it as an obligation (above 1:6).
lest sleep overcome him and he be found sleeping all night. Out of great fatigue he will not wake and will not pray.
and it is permitted to get a haircut and enter the bathhouse close to Shacharit. From dawn onward, which is the beginning of the time of the prayer (above 3:7).
he stops and prays. He interrupts his study for the prayer.
his Torah is his craft. It is his only occupation.
one engaged in the needs of the community. Matters that the public needs, and for this reason he cannot pray (and compare Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:5).
only because of danger to life. For most commandments are set aside before it (for the principle see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 5:1).
the king of Israel... he does not answer him. Despite the obligation to honor him (compare Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:15-17).
a brigand. A dangerous robber.
he shortens. And finishes the prayer quickly, so that he will not have to interrupt his prayer.
deadly. Poisonous.
women and slaves. Although they are exempt from time-bound positive commandments, they are obligated in prayer, because it is not time-dependent but a constant obligation (see above 1:2).
and minors are obligated in prayer. For they are trained in this mitzvah (see also Hilchot Keriat Shema 4:1, Hilchot Tefillin 4:13, Hilchot Mezuzah 5:10).
and anyone who is exempt from the reading of the Shema. Such as a groom and those occupied with a corpse (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 4:1-6).
even though the bier has no need of them. Because they are not carrying the deceased.
are exempt from prayer. Because they cannot focus properly, due to the preoccupation of the funeral (compare ibid. 4:4).
when the Sages instituted these words of prayer. The fixed text of the prayer (above 1:4).
to bless them every day. To thank the Creator for important deeds and events, so as to remember Him always (Hilchot Berakhot 1:3-4).
who casts the bonds of sleep upon my eyes and gives light to the pupil of the eye. That the eyes are bound by sleep, yet do not permanently cease to function.
and let my bed be whole before You. That there be no blemish in my conduct and in my descendants (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:4).
and enlighten my eyes lest I sleep the sleep of death. Continue the function of my eyes, so that I will awaken from my sleep.
who gives light to the whole world. That the light throughout the world exists by Your merit.
the first section of the Shema. The "Shema" passage (Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:2); no more is needed, since he has already fulfilled the mitzvah of the evening Shema.
sleep overcomes him. He knows he will fall asleep immediately (see ibid. 2:3).
verses of mercy. Verses containing prayer and a request for protection during sleep.
when he awakes at the end of his sleep. When he wakes and rises from sleep.
he blesses while on his bed. While still on his bed, he gives thanks for the return of his soul to his body.
pure. Clean, without sin.
You created it. In the creation of man, of whom it says "And God created man..." (Genesis 1:27).
You formed it. In the forming of man from the earth, of whom it says "And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground..." (Genesis 2:7).
You breathed it into me. You breathed the soul into the body, as it says further in that verse, "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life."
You preserve it within me. You keep it within me, lest I die.
to take it. To take it away when I die.
to restore it to me in the time to come. At the time of the resurrection of the dead.
who restores souls to dead corpses. For You revive the dead, and awakening from sleep is similar to that.
the voice of the rooster. The one that crows at dawn.
who gave the rooster understanding to distinguish. For He gave the rooster the ability to discern at the first appearance of light.
his sheet. A special garment for covering the head.
who crowns Israel with splendor. For God's way of adorning Israel is expressed in the covering of the head.
when he passes his hands over his eyes. To remove the dirt.
who opens the eyes of the blind. For God's way of opening the eyes of the blind is expressed in restoring sight after sleep.
who releases the bound. For God's way of releasing prisoners from jail is expressed in restoring the ability to move.
who spreads the earth upon the waters. For God's way of stabilizing the ground is appreciated when a person walks on it.
who straightens the bent. For God's way of helping the poor and raising them up is expressed in a person's ability to stand upright.
when he washes his hands. This is the washing of the hands for the Shema and prayer (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:1, above 4:2, Hilchot Berakhot 6:2; and see further below halachah 10).
that You accustom me. Help me to become used to them.
and let the good inclination rule over me. Let the good inclination dominate me.
and grant my portion in Your Torah. That my inheritance be in the Torah.

he says before he enters: Be honored, honored ones. An apology to the angels who accompany a person at all times, for being about to do something not honorable, and a request that they wait until he finishes.

openings and openings, and cavities and cavities etc.. Some organs are open and perforated and some are hollow and closed; if the closed one were opened or the open one closed, it would be impossible to live.
who heals all flesh. For the expelling of waste from the body is healing for it.
and acts wondrously. Performs miracles.
who girds Israel with strength. For God's way of strengthening Israel and helping them overcome their enemies is expressed in putting on the belt (which is like girding oneself with weapons).
who has provided for all my needs. For shoes are an essential addition to a person's needs, and this blessing includes all the things he needs.
who prepares the steps of man. God's guiding of a person in all his ways is expressed when he walks on the road.
and a person blesses every day etc.. These three blessings are for the full obligation in the commandments, unlike a gentile, slave and woman, who are exempt from part of them.
they have no order. There is no connection between the blessings, and they are not a single unit (compare the custom mentioned below, halachah 9).
at its time. At the time it occurs.
while still on his bed. Before he gets down from it.
if he heard the rooster's voice afterward etc.. Even though in the order given (above halachah 4) this blessing appears first.
that he was not obligated in. That the matter for which one blesses did not happen to him.
he slept in his clothes. He slept dressed in his garments, and did not need to dress upon rising.
barefoot. Without shoes.
on Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av, when there is no washing. For washing is forbidden then due to the severity of the fast (see Hilchot Shevitat Asor 3:1, Hilchot Ta'aniyot 5:10).
who removes sleep. Which is recited on washing the face (above halachah 4).
in most of our cities. In most of the places where Jews live.
unless he was obligated in it. As above, halachah 7.
to read the Torah. To study Torah.
before he reads the Shema. But after reading the Shema he does not recite a blessing over words of Torah, since their blessing is included in the blessings of the Shema.
and commanded us concerning the words of Torah. He commanded us to engage in Torah.
make pleasant etc.. A request that the words of Torah be sweet and pleasant in our mouths.
and in the mouths. And in the mouths.
who chose us from among all the nations etc.. A blessing of praise and thanksgiving for the choosing of Israel and for the very privilege and honor of receiving the Torah (see below 12:5).
a person must recite these three blessings. Because of the mitzvah to study Torah every day (Hilchot Talmud Torah 1:8).
to read the Priestly Blessing. The verses of the blessing, "May the Lord bless you and keep you..." (Numbers 6:24-26).
Command the children of Israel. The passage commanding the daily offering.
and they read chapters or halachot from the Mishnah or from the Baraitot. In order to study from the Oral Torah as well.
Psalms. Tehillim.
a Psalm of praise of David. A psalm of praise to God for His greatness and kindness, whose verses are arranged in alphabetical order.
to the end of the book. These are five further chapters of praise, which begin and end with the word "Hallelujah."
to read verses before and after them. Verses of praise, most gathered from the Book of Psalms (for the details of the verses and blessings see Seder HaTefillot, 4-7).
Baruch She'amar. An introductory blessing to the recitation of praise, which says that God is praised through the psalms David wrote.
Yishtabach. A concluding blessing for the verses of praise, which says that it is fitting to use every language of praise to glorify the Creator.
he blesses over the reading of the Shema and reads the Shema. For after this preparation they turn to the obligatory prayers (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:5-6).
the Song of the Sea. The song of the Israelites and their thanks to God for the miracle of the splitting of the Red Sea and the drowning of the Egyptians in it (Exodus 15:1-21).
the song of Ha'azinu. Which Moses taught the Israelites, describing Israel's sufferings and redemption (Deuteronomy 32:1-43).
between day and night. For the blessings of day and night are counted together for this purpose.

the twenty-three blessings we counted in this chapter. The eighteen morning blessings (halachot 3-6), the three Torah blessings (halachah 11), and the two blessings before and after the Pesukei DeZimra (halachah 12).
and the seven blessings of the Shema. Three in the morning and four in the evening (Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:5).
and when he wraps himself in tzitzit he blesses. See also Hilchot Tzitzit 3:8.
and when he puts on his tefillin he blesses. See Hilchot Tefillin 4:4-5; all together they are thirty-two blessings.
and three prayers... eighteen blessings. Which together make fifty-four blessings.
and over food, one at the beginning. The blessing of HaMotzi.
and three at the end. Birkat HaMazon, which originally consists of three blessings (see Hilchot Berakhot 2:1).
and over water. That he drank after the meal (see Hilchot De'ot 4:2).
that they instituted the blessing concerning the heretics. And they added it to the eighteen blessings of the prayer (above 2:1).
and they added HaTov VeHaMetiv in Birkat HaMazon. They added it in the days of the Sages of the Mishnah (Hilchot Berakhot 2:1), after the destruction of Betar.
five additional blessings. Which are three from the three prayers and two from Birkat HaMazon.
for the prayer has seven blessings. For the middle blessing deals with the sanctity of the day and replaces the middle blessings recited on every day (see above 2:5).
if he was not obligated etc.. As above, halachah 7.
and he blesses before and after it. Before it, "who creates the fruit of the ground" or "of the tree," and after it, "who creates many living beings" (Hilchot Berakhot 8:1).
the order of prayers. The arrangement of prayers for an individual (for communal prayer see below chapter 9).
and he recites these blessings. The blessings mentioned in this chapter (halachot 3-6, 11).
and he reads the Zemirot. The chapters of Psalms that they customarily recite (halachah 12).
and he omits the Kedushah. For Kedushah is not said without ten (Hilchot Tefillah 8:4), including this Kedushah of the first blessing of the Shema.
and he prays standing as we said. Above 5:2.
he sits and falls on his face and supplicates. For they were accustomed to fall on their faces while seated and not by prostrating (see above 5:13-14).
and afterward he reads Tehillah LeDavid. For they are careful to say this chapter three times every day.
and he supplicates as much as he is able. For the details of the verses of supplication see Seder HaTefillot, 35.
and he departs to his affairs. He turns to his business.
he begins to read Tehillah LeDavid while seated. And this psalm is the introduction to the prayer.
while seated. Sitting.
the prayer of the congregation is always heard. Is accepted at any time.
sinners. Sinful people.
as long as he can pray with a congregation. As long as he is able to do so.
a person should arrive early and stay late. He should come in the morning and in the evening.
at any time. Even not at the time of the congregational prayer.
he is called a bad neighbor. Who does not make visits, although his house is nearby.
to run to the synagogue. To show the dearness of the mitzvah.
he should not take a long stride. He should not walk fast with big steps.
he walks little by little. Slowly.
he should enter the measure of two doorways. He should enter the synagogue and move inward from the door the distance of another doorway.
the doorposts of my doors. A hint at two doorways.
the house of study is greater than the synagogue. For its sanctity is greater (below 11:14; Hilchot Talmud Torah 4:9), and likewise its merit regarding prayer is greater.
provided that he prays communal prayer there. For there is no advantage to an individual's prayer in the house of study over communal prayer in the synagogue.
he prays aloud and everyone hears. The Amidah.
adults and free persons. Who are not slaves or minors.
and the prayer leader is one of them. He too is counted as one of the ten.
provided that most of the ten have not prayed. Those who have prayed are only to complete the majority.
Kedushah. Said in the repetition of the Amidah (see below 9:4), as well as that said in the blessing of the luminaries (see above 7:17), and in Seder HaYom (below 9:5-6).
and the Torah is not read etc.. For the reading, with the special blessings for these readings (see below 12:5, 12:15), is done only in a congregation (12:3).
one person should not recite the blessings of the Shema etc.. The first part of the communal prayer, which is the Shema and its blessings (see below 9:1).
leads. Recites the two blessings of the Shema that precede it.

Kaddish. A prayer of praise that the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, be magnified and blessed in the world. It is said at the beginning of the communal prayer and at its end (see below 9:1, 9:6; for the text see Seder HaTefillot, 29).
raise their hands. To bless with the Priestly Blessing (see below chapters 14-15).
and the kohanim are counted in the minyan. They too are counted as part of the ten (see below 15:9).
How long shall this congregation etc.. This verse refers to those spies who spoke ill of the Land of Israel, and calls them a "congregation."
and they were ten, since Joshua and Caleb had left. For originally there were twelve men, and these two did not take part in the spies' counsel, so it emerges that "congregation" means ten.
and any matter of holiness. Of those matters enumerated above.
if they began them with ten etc.. If they began the matter of holiness in the presence of a minyan of ten, and some left in the middle.
even though they are not permitted. For it is forbidden for them to do so.
the rest should finish. Those who remained should finish the thing they began.
in one place. In the same domain.

a small courtyard that was breached along its full width into a large courtyard. They adjoin each other and the whole wall between them was demolished, but looking from within the large courtyard, walls are visible on both sides of the breach, because it is wider than the small courtyard.
nine in the large one and one in the small one combine. Because the small one is subordinate to the large one.

nine in the small one and one in the large one do not combine. For the large one is not subordinate to the small one, and does not join with it because of the partition formed by the walls at the sides of the breach between them; therefore the one standing in it is not drawn after those standing in the small one.
they fulfil their obligation. For the prayer leader too is drawn after the majority of the congregation.
for he is separated from them. Apart from them.
posts on either side. Partial partitions on both sides, so that it is evident that there is a partition with an opening.
like a corner. A corner.
if there was filth. Beside which it is forbidden to pray or recite the Shema (above 4:8, Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:4).
it is forbidden to pray and recite the Shema in the small one. For it is like a corner of the large one, and in the same domain.
a bad smell. Which also must be kept away from (see ibid. 3:12).
because it is separated from it. Separate, and if the filth is in a different domain one may recite and pray (ibid. 3:9).
the prayer leader. The cantor who prays aloud.
fulfils the obligation of the many. So that they do not need to pray themselves.
as if they prayed. As though they had prayed (see Hilchot Berakhot 1:11).
with one who does not know how to pray. And therefore can fulfil his obligation through the prayer leader's prayer.
except for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur of the Jubilee. For on these days the Musaf prayer is lengthened, and it has nine blessings: Malkhuyot, Zikhronot and Shofarot (above 2:6-8).
and most of those who know them cannot focus their minds on them. Because of their great length.
the greatest in the congregation in wisdom and deeds. Who is great in wisdom and has good deeds.
his voice is pleasant and he is practiced in reading. With a beautiful voice and skilled in reading the verses of Scripture.
whose beard has not filled out. Who has not yet reached the age at which all the beard hair grows (Responsa of Rambam 177).
out of respect for the congregation. For it is not to their honor that such a young man be the prayer leader.
but he may lead the Shema etc.. For one who leads the Shema is not considered a prayer leader, and it suffices that he be obligated in the commandments in order to fulfil the obligation of others.
and likewise one who stammers. Who garbles the reading.
one who pronounces ayin as alef etc.. Who does not distinguish between them.
to pronounce the letters properly. To articulate them correctly.
and the teacher appoints one of his students. The one whom the teacher considers fit to be the prayer leader.
the blind person. Blind.
may lead the Shema. Although he does not see the luminaries, he blesses over them because he benefits from their existence.
but one whose shoulders are bare... until he is wrapped. Covered. For so it is fitting for the prayer leader, and so is the way of the Sages and their students in their prayer (above 5:5).

goes down before the ark. In the middle of the front of the synagogue there is an ark in which the Torah scroll is placed, and the prayer leader stands on the ground with his face toward it and his back to the congregation (see below 11:3-4).
may His great Name be blessed. May His great Name (of the Holy One, blessed be He) be blessed.
and they answer Amen at the end of Kaddish. And also in several places during it (see Seder HaTefillot, 30).
and he leads the Shema. He recites the Shema with its blessings (see above 8:5).
and one who knows how to bless and read recites with him. And if he does not know, the prayer leader fulfils his obligation for him (see above 8:9).
and everyone stands immediately and prays silently. Immediately after "Ga'al Yisrael," in order to join redemption to prayer (above 7:17).
stands silent until the prayer leader prays. He waits without disturbing those praying, until the prayer leader finishes the silent prayer.
and he should stand in the place he has reached. And not return to the place where he stood, until they reach the Kedushah (below halachah 4).
to fulfil the obligation of one who did not pray. Who does not know how to pray (above 8:9).
and everyone stands etc.. Everyone answers Amen, whether they prayed or are fulfilling their obligation through the prayer leader's prayer (see Hilchot Berakhot 1:13).

and he recites Kedushah in the third blessing. He begins the blessing with a call to sanctify the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the world, like the angels (for the text of the Kedushah see Seder HaTefillot, 26).
they bow slightly. They bend a little, but not in a full bow (compare above 5:12).
for we thank You. All these praises are in addition to the thanksgiving that was in the prayer.
"Modim, Modim". For it would seem as if he is thanking two authorities (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:11).
that he complete the whole prayer. That he finish the repetition of the Amidah.
he sits and falls on his face etc.. This is the falling on the face (see above 5:13-15, 7:17).
in the way they answered at first. "Amen, yehei shmei rabba" (as above halachah 1).
and one called to the other. This is the beginning of the verse of the Kedushah.
and they answer. The congregation answers and completes the Kedushah, as is done in the Amidah (above halachah 4).
and he again reads the Kedushah in translation... to make it understood to the people. He translates the verses into Aramaic so that it is understood by all (see below 12:10).
these are called Seder HaYom. For the reading of these verses was instituted originally as a fixed daily study order.
and afterward he supplicates with words of supplication and verses of mercy. For details see Seder HaTefillot, 35.
they answer in their usual way and depart. They answer "Amen, yehei shmei rabba" etc., and then go about their business.
He who had mercy on a bird's nest etc.. For He commanded in the Torah to send away the mother and then take the young (Deuteronomy 22:6; and see Hilchot Shechitah 13:1).
that one not slaughter it and its young etc.. For this was forbidden in the Torah (Leviticus 22:28; and see Hilchot Shechitah 12:1).
will have mercy on us. Just as He commands compassionate conduct toward animals.
and they are not mercies. They do not stem from compassion.
at all. In general.
in epithets. Expressions of praise.
and the mighty and the strong. Synonyms for strong.
for a person has no power to reach the end of His praises etc.. A person cannot recite all of God's praises.
he says what Moses our teacher said. The way he described God's greatness in the Torah: "the great, the mighty and the awesome" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and does not add to these epithets.
and He is merciful etc.. Introductory verses to the prayer (compare above 7:18).
as he did in Shacharit. Above, halachot 3-4.
and he supplicates a little while seated. While sitting, as above halachah 5.
to lead the Shema. To read the Shema with its blessings (as above halachah 1).
since the evening prayer is not obligatory. For it was not instituted corresponding to the daily offering (above 1:6).
blessings in vain. Without need, and it is forbidden to do so (Berakhot 1:15).

for there is no one here who is obligated in them in order to fulfil his obligation. For the repetition of the prayer is meant to fulfil the obligation of one who is not proficient (above halachah 3).
one blessing that is a summary of the seven. Which is the essence of the seven blessings.
Maker. Creator.
Shield of the fathers by His word. For He promised the fathers to save them from every harm.
who gives rest to His people. Who granted them a day of rest.
for He took pleasure in them. He chose them.
the source of blessings. The origin of the blessings.
he does not pray the seven. He does not repeat the prayer in full.
for most of the people. Many people.
and there may be someone who came late etc.. Among the congregation there may be a person who was late, who will finish his prayer later than the rest of the congregation.
and come into danger. For it is dangerous to go out at night alone.
the prayer leader does not... mention the matter of the day. He does not conclude with a blessing that mentions the sanctity of the particular day.
for he is not obligated today in this prayer. For it is not part of that day's obligation, but was instituted solely in honor of Shabbat.
and they pray Musaf silently. And the custom was that after Shacharit they read the Torah, and afterward they pray Musaf (see below 12:20).
and they do not say Kedushah or supplications. Of Seder HaYom (above halachah 5).
he says Seder HaYom after the Musaf prayer. For those days they were not accustomed to defer them to the Minchah prayer.
and afterward he recites Havdalah. For Havdalah is recited in the synagogue, to fulfil the obligation of the many (compare Hilchot Shabbat 29:8).

he must go back and pray with concentration. For "any prayer without concentration is not prayer" (above 4:15), because prayer is "service of the heart" and is based on the intention of the heart (above 1:1).

and if he concentrated during the first blessing etc.. For it is the beginning of the prayer, in which the relationship between the one praying and God is described. And the essential concentration is that he see himself as standing before the Divine Presence (above 4:16).
one who erred etc.. For the first three blessings are considered a single unit, and so are the last ones (see above 1:4).
he returns to Avodah. The first of the last blessings.
and completes his prayer in order. From that blessing onward.
in this manner. In the same way.
when he prays silently. Together with the whole congregation (above 9:2).
because of the burden on the congregation. For they would have to wait for him until he finishes the second prayer.
he relies on the prayer etc.. That his prayer aloud will count as the repetition regarding the error.
and this is that if he errs in it he always returns. It is the prayer aloud that the prayer leader repeats if he errs (as above halachah 1).
and became flustered. Became confused.
and did not know where to begin. He forgot how the blessing begins.
and waited an hour. He waited a while and did not remember what to say.
another should stand in his place. Another person should replace him in his prayer.
they do not wait for him. Until he lingers, as above.
lest heresy has been thrown into him. Lest he has become a heretic, and for that reason he avoids the blessing against the heretics (and see above 2:1).
if he began it, they wait for him an hour. As with other who err; for if he began it, there is no suspicion of heresy.
and the second should not be reluctant at that time. Rather, he should agree to replace the prayer leader immediately.
and from where does he begin. The second prayer leader, who stood in the place of the one who erred.
but if he erred in one of the first three etc.. Which are as a single unit (as above halachah 1).
because my clothes are dyed. And he wants to pray only in white garments, as they served in the Temple.
even in white he should not pass before the ark in that prayer. They do not allow him to be prayer leader, since such insistence is of the ways of the heretics.
because I have a sandal on my foot. And he wants to pray barefoot, as was done in the Temple.

one who was in doubt... does not return and pray. For the number of prayers and their text is not a Torah commandment but of the Sages (see above 1:1), and a doubt regarding the words of the Sages is resolved leniently.
unless... with the intention that it be a freewill offering. He may return and pray, if he intends it to be a freewill prayer.
for if an individual wishes etc.. Just as an individual may bring freewill offerings on any weekday (see above 1:9-10).
and he remembered that he had already prayed, he stops. For he is not obligated in that prayer, and it is forbidden to recite an unnecessary blessing (see Hilchot Berakhot 1:15).
and if it was the evening prayer etc.. Which is an optional prayer (above 1:6).

but with the intention that it is not obligatory. That he intended from the outset to add a prayer he is not obligated in. And although Israel accepted it upon themselves as an obligation, it is originally optional (see above 3:6-7, 6:7, 9:9).
in Musaf he stops even in the middle of the blessing etc.. For the blessings of request are not connected to the Musaf prayer at all.

he returns to the beginning. Because he erred in not mentioning God's might in giving rain, at the time suitable for rainfall (see above 2:15). And he must return to the beginning of the prayer because he erred in one of the first three (above halachah 1).
and if he mentioned the dew he does not return. For he mentioned God's might, who gives water to the world.
and if he erred in the summer... he returns to the beginning. For rain in the summer is a sign of a curse.
for dew is not withheld and needs no request. For the mention of might is like a request, and therefore omitting the dew is not a complete error.
who forgot the request in the blessing of the years. He did not mention the request for rain in the winter (above 2:16).
he asks for the rains in Shome'a Tefillah. For in this blessing he may request all his needs (above 6:3, and see 2:17).
he returns to the blessing of the years. Which is the place of this request.
he returns and prays a second time. Because he erred in an important matter.
Ya'aleh VeYavo. The special addition for festivals, which is a request to be remembered before God on these days. It is said in the blessing of Avodah (above 2:10-11).
words of supplication after his prayer etc.. Additional requests after the end of the prayer, which a person may lengthen (above 6:2).
Ma'ariv of Rosh Chodesh... he does not return. For the month is not sanctified at night (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 2:8).
he returns and prays if he erred in the same way. In a similar error, and there is no difference in their laws.
because of the burden on the congregation. For they would have to wait until he prays again from the beginning.
the Musaf prayers are before him. And when necessary, this mention suffices.
the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur. During which they add special additions to the text of the prayer (see above 2:18-19).
and he concluded... the holy God. Instead of "the holy King."
he returns to the beginning. As in the law of one who errs in the first three.
he returns to the beginning of the blessing. As in the law of one who errs in one of the middle blessings.
Havdalah in Chonen HaDa'at. On Motzaei Shabbat or Motzaei Yom Tov (above 2:12).
he completes his prayer and need not return. For he recites Havdalah afterward over a cup of wine (see Hilchot Shabbat 29:6).
who did not mention Al HaNissim on Chanukah and Purim. In the blessing of Hoda'ah (above 2:13).
and Aneinu in the prayer of a fast day. Which an individual says in the blessing Shome'a Tefillah, and the prayer leader says between Go'el and Rofe (above 2:14).
he does not return and pray. For these are additions that are not essential.
and if he remembered before he moved his feet. He may attach the prayer "Aneinu" to the supplications after the prayer.
may they be acceptable etc.. It is the verse that concludes the prayer (above 2:9).
he prays two evening prayers of Shabbat. Even though the make-up prayer differs from the prayer he forgot (on the make-up prayer see above 3:8-10).
and likewise on a festival. If he did not pray Minchah on the eve of the festival, he prays two evening prayers of the festival.
he recites Havdalah in the first and not in the second. For the first is the prayer in its proper time, and after it he prays the make-up prayer (above 3:8).

and if he recited Havdalah in both or did not recite it in one of them, he has fulfilled his obligation. For there is no flaw in an extra Havdalah, and even if he did not recite it at all he has fulfilled his obligation (above halachah 14).
because he put it first in the prayer that is the evening prayer. For the Havdalah is a sign that the second one specifically is the evening prayer.
even Shacharit and Musaf. Which are usually prayed one after the other (see above 9:13).
so that his mind settles. The time needed for his mind to settle so he can supplicate properly (see above 4:16).
it is forbidden for one who prays etc.. Rather, he must pray together with the congregation (and see further above 6:2).
to begin and finish. The Amidah.
he answers Kedushah with the congregation and prays the rest of the prayer by himself. Without regard to the pace of the prayer leader.
he should not interrupt etc.. For one should not interrupt the prayer for anything (see above 6:9), not even for matters of holiness.
he must say in the other blessings. For one does not interrupt the prayer to answer other blessings.
in which there are ten Israelites. And they can pray as a congregation (above 8:4).
and the townspeople may compel one another. They may force one another to participate in the payments for building and purchasing (see also Hilchot Shekhenim 6:1).
and to buy for themselves a Torah scroll, Prophets and Writings. So that they can read from them in public and study from them.
at the highest point of the city. In the highest place in the city.
and they raise it. The building itself.
and the doors of the synagogue are opened only to the east etc.. Just as the entrance of the Tabernacle, and of the Temple, faced east.
and they build in it a hekhal. A kind of small chamber in which Torah scrolls are stored.
in the direction toward which they pray in that city. In the same direction that they face when praying.
a bimah in the synagogue. A raised structure in the center of the synagogue.
words of admonition. Words of moral instruction.

and when they place the ark in which there is a Torah scroll etc.. Sometimes they take the Torah scroll out of the hekhal and place it in a cabinet (the Holy Ark), and they place the cabinet in the center of the front of the synagogue.
and its face is toward the people. Its front side (the opening) faces the congregation.
the elders. The Torah scholars.
row before row. One after another.
the faces of all the people toward the holy place etc.. And all the rows face the same direction, which is the direction of prayer.
on the ground before the ark. He stands on the floor, and not on a raised place (above 5:6-7; and see above 9:1).
they sweep. They sweep.
and sprinkle. They sprinkle water, in order to clean them.
and in the West. In the communities of North Africa.
in Shinar and the Land of Israel. Babylonia and the Land of Israel.
lamps. Lamps.
and in the cities of Edom. The countries of Europe.
they do not behave lightheadedly in them etc.. Rather, they honor the place by behaving seriously.
make use of. Use.
and one does not enter them etc.. It is forbidden to use them as shelter from the elements.
they are permitted to eat and drink in them in case of need. When they have no other option.
and one does not calculate accounts in them. For this too is an undignified use.
a public eulogy. Which is a communal need.
for all the people gather and come on their account. In honor of those sages who take part in the eulogy.
he should not make it a thoroughfare etc.. It is forbidden to use it as a shortcut.
to shorten the way. To cut the route short.
for it is forbidden to enter them except for a mitzvah purpose. As will be explained in the following halachot (and see also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:2).
to call a child. To call a boy, for the children would study in the synagogue, as below.
and let him read a little. Verses from Scripture.
a tradition. A halachah from the Oral Torah.
so that he does not enter solely for his own business. But for the sake of a mitzvah.
to one of the children. Who sit and study in the synagogue.
he is permitted to exit through the door opposite him to shorten his way. For it is permitted to enter a synagogue for a mitzvah purpose.

and a person is permitted to enter the synagogue... and if he needs to spit he spits etc.. Although all these things are forbidden on the Temple Mount (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:2), that is because there is a special duty of reverence there. But in a synagogue they are permitted, as they are not matters of disgrace.
and in his apundah. A garment worn against the flesh that absorbs sweat, with no other garment over it.
they retain their sanctity. Their holiness is not nullified, even though they are no longer built.
as it says. In the passage of rebuke, as a punishment for violating the covenant with God.
and I will lay waste your sanctuaries. I will destroy and make desolate the holy places (and see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:16).
and just as they treat them when they are inhabited. With respect, in all the matters enumerated above from halachah 5 onward.
so that the people will see them etc.. For the growth of weeds is a sign of the building's lowly state, and will stir in the hearts of those who see it the desire to restore it.
demolish. Tear down.
in its place. In that very place.
even one wall of it. One of the synagogue's walls that must be rebuilt while the other walls remain standing.
in what case is this said. That the old structure must be left until the new one is completed.
whose foundations have not been ruined. Of the old building, and it can be left standing.
and they begin to build it quickly, by day and by night. So that they can finish it as fast as possible.
a house of study. A place for Torah study.
greater. Greater (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 4:9, above 8:3).

and one elevates in holiness and does not lower. One may increase the level of sanctity, but not reduce it (for this rule see also Hilchot Tzitzit 1:7, Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:16, Hilchot Keli HaMikdash 4:21, Hilchot Sanhedrin 17:9).
the townspeople who sold the synagogue. Under the conditions that will be explained below, halachah 16 onward.
they may take with its proceeds an ark etc.. For in all of these there is an elevation in the level of sanctity.
an ark. In which the Torah scroll is placed (above halachah 3).
wrappers. That are wrapped around holy books.

Chumashim. A Torah scroll divided into separate books, which does not have the sanctity of a Torah scroll and is unfit for public reading, and is used for the instruction of children (see Hilchot Sefer Torah 7:14, 10:1).
and likewise with their surplus. For even what is left over from the sale of these items, after buying something holy, may not be used to buy something of lesser sanctity.
and they wished to change. The purpose of the money.
they may change the surplus to whatever they wish. Even for purposes that are not an elevation in holiness.
like a synagogue. In terms of their level of sanctity they are like a synagogue, because they are regularly used for prayer.
the curtain over the ark in which they keep the books. Which is hung before the Holy Ark as an ornament.
like the wrappers of the books. Because sometimes it is used for the Torah scroll itself, like the wrappers of the books.
and if they stipulated concerning them. If the community stipulated in advance that sanctity would not apply to these items in this way, the stipulation is effective.
villages. Small settlements.
the synagogue of the large cities. Major cities, where many who are not locals come to pray.
to the town. To that city.
they must stipulate with the buyer etc.. That it may not be sold for purposes that involve disgrace.
a bathhouse. Used for laundry.
and if the seven good men of the city stipulated etc.. If it is known and publicly announced that the place was sold, and its sanctity has been transferred to the money (as below, halachah 20).
seven good men of the city. Officially chosen representatives appointed over the city's affairs.
permitted. For it is no longer a disgrace in the eyes of the many.
over the surplus of the money. From the sale of holy items, above halachah 14.
one person. Who will be appointed over what is done in the city.
so too they give it as a gift. For if they gave it away, its law is as if they sold it.
for if the community had no benefit etc.. Presumably the community derives some benefit from such a gift, and since there is a return for the gift, it is like a sale.
they do not rent it etc.. For the sanctity of a synagogue is removed only when it is transferred to the proceeds.
to lend them. To lend them out.
they pray in it on fast days. On the special fasts held in years of drought (see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 4:1).
and on ma'amadot. Times when the people of that place gather to pray on behalf of all Israel (see Hilchot Keli HaMikdash chapter 6).
because the gathering is large. Many people assemble.
and it was not set for prayer. The street is not designated for prayer, but is used for it for lack of choice.
like a person who prays in his house. For he does not dedicate his house to the sanctity of a synagogue, and its main use is not for prayer.
in public. With ten (below halachah 3), and this reading is combined with communal prayer (below halachah 20).
because of the idlers. People with nothing to do, so that they will engage in Torah at midday on Shabbat.
and he too instituted etc.. For until his time there was no fixed number of readers and no fixed length for the reading.
three people. Each of whom reads a few verses himself before the congregation (for the number of readers on other days see below halachah 16).
they conclude with the Prophets. After the Torah reading they finish with a reading from the books of the Prophets (below chapters 13-15).
and they conclude with the Prophets only on Shabbatot etc.. For these are days with leisure.
adults and free persons. Who are not slaves or minors (see also above 8:4).
and "Vayedaber" is counted. The verse "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying" is counted as one of the ten verses, although it is merely an introduction to what follows.
and they do not begin a passage with fewer than three verses. One does not begin reading a new passage unless one reads at least three verses in it.

and they do not leave fewer than three verses in a passage. One does not end a reading when fewer than three verses remain from the stopping point to the end of the passage (for the details of the passages see Hilchot Sefer Torah chapter 8).
two read three each. Each of them reads three verses.
and whether the first reader read four etc.. For in each of the three aliyot there is a certain merit, because of which it is fit for the longer reading.
and he looks at the place where he is going to read. So that the blessing refers to the verses he is about to read.
who chose us etc.. The introductory blessing for the reading, on the privilege and honor of Israel in receiving the Torah (it is one of the three Torah blessings said every day, above 7:10).
he rolls up the scroll. He closes it, since he has finished reading.
who gave us the Torah of truth etc.. The concluding blessing, praising the Torah itself as true and eternal.
until Amen finishes from the mouth of the congregation. Until the congregation finishes saying Amen to his blessing, so that they hear him reading (see below 14:5).
he read and erred. Did not read precisely as required.
two in the Torah. Together, because neither one's voice is heard clearly.
another should stand in his place. He replaces him.
that the greatest in the congregation tell him to read. For a person may not honor himself.
and even the synagogue attendant or the head of the synagogue etc.. The beadle and the synagogue administrator too are not permitted to read without being invited.
he may skip from place to place on one subject. He may skip, in the course of reading, to another passage if it deals with the same topic.

Acharei Mot and Ach BeAsor in the portion Emor El HaKohanim. These are the passages that the High Priest read on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 3:10; and see below 13:11), and since both deal with one matter, the service of Yom Kippur, he may skip.
that he not read by heart. That he read only from the scroll.
for it is forbidden to read other than from the written text. For this is not considered reading.
a word. A word.

and he must not linger over the skipping, etc.. The permission to skip is conditional on the skipping time matching the translation of the last verse read (below 11), so that the congregation need not wait during the skipping (see below 23).
to speak. To talk.
between one man and another. In the pause between the readers.
and one who engages in Torah constantly, etc.. If Torah is his sole occupation and he studies it all the time, his occupation takes precedence over hearing the Torah read in public (see above 6:8).
so that they will understand the matter. Because they did not understand the language of Scripture well (see Nehemiah 8:5-8; and see also above 9:5).
he reads only one verse, etc.. And he stops after reading each verse so that it can be translated.
and the reader may not read to the translator more than one verse. Because this burdens the translator, who translates orally.
the reader may not raise his voice, etc.. For something similar see Hilchot Talmud Torah 4:3.
and the translator may not translate, etc.. So that neither drowns out the other's voice.
and he may not translate from the text. From a book.

and the reader may not help the translator, etc.. To remind him of the translation of what he read, since if he helps, the people will think that the translation too is written in the Torah scroll itself.
and a minor. One who is not obligated in the commandments (for its definition see Hilchot Ishut 2:10).
translates for the adult. On behalf of the adult, when the adult is reading.
and it is not honorable, etc.. Since the reader is more important than the translator.
two as one. As is the law for the reader (above 5:6).
and not all the verses are translated in public. There are verses that are not translated.
the incident of Reuben. Which relates that he lay with his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22). It is not translated out of respect for Reuben (see Hilchot Sotah 3:2).

and the Priestly Blessing. The verses of blessing that the priests were commanded to use to bless Israel (Numbers 6:24-26; and see its text in the commentary below 14:3). Translating it literally might mislead the public into thinking that God shows favoritism and does not insist on strict justice.
and the incident of the calf, etc.. Since these verses mention that Aaron made the calf, they refrain from translating it out of respect for him.
and the incident of Amnon. The son of King David, who deceitfully raped Tamar, the king's daughter (II Samuel chapter 13).
is neither read nor translated. The verse that attributes him to his father is not read, out of respect for the royal house.
must first read from the Torah. Out of respect for the Torah, so that the reading from the Prophets is subordinate to the Torah.
and he may not read the haftarah from the Prophets until the Torah scroll has been rolled up. That is, it is wrapped and closed (below 18), out of respect for the Torah.
from twenty-one verses. Corresponding to seven aliyot of three verses each.
the subject is complete. The topic has ended.
and the translator translates, it suffices. That is enough.
and even two may translate. Since they are not so strict about the translation of the Prophets (compare above 11).
and he may skip from one subject to another. To a different topic (compare above 5:8).
but he may not skip from one prophet to another. Because this may cause confusion.
in the Twelve Prophets. The twelve books of the prophets that were joined together and are considered a single book.
he may not skip from the end of the book to its beginning. Even within the same prophet.
he must not linger over the skipping, etc.. Similar to the law of one who skips in the Torah (above 5:8).
he may read three verses to the translator. He is permitted to do so (compare above 5:10), since they are not so strict about translating the Prophets.
three passages. Separate paragraphs.
who chose, etc.. A blessing of praise for God's choosing the Torah, Israel, and the prophets.
the God who is faithful in all His words. That all the words of prophecy are true and are fulfilled.
who builds Jerusalem. A plea for mercy for Israel and for Jerusalem.
Shield of David. A request for the restoration of the strength of David's kingship (for the full text of the blessings see Seder HaTefillot, 63).
as he concludes in the prayer. In the middle blessing of the sanctity of the day (see Seder HaTefillot, 55).
on Shabbat morning they read seven, etc.. Because each of the days mentioned is holier than the one after it.
but they may add. If they want additional people to read.
they read three... and do not add to it. Because there is no free time on these occasions, so they do not lengthen the reading beyond what was instituted.

a woman may not read in public, out of respect for the congregation. Because it is not respectful to them that a woman, who is obligated in fewer commandments than men, knows how to read while they do not (for a similar idea see Hilchot Berakhot 5:15, Hilchot Ma'aser 10:5).
one who knows how to read. Who knows how to read from the book.
and knows to Whom one gives blessings. That blessings are made to God, who is the Creator of the world (see Hilchot Berakhot 5:7).
counts toward the number of readers. Completes the number of the seven who are called up.
the one who completes. The one called up who completed the Torah reading.
does not go up. Because the Kaddish marks the end of the reading (below 20; and see Seder HaTefillot, 28).

a congregation in which only one person knew how to read. For by law, the person called to the Torah must himself read the verses of his aliyah before the congregation (see Rulings and Opinions above 1).
goes up, reads, goes down and sits, etc.. The one who knows how to read goes up for all the aliyot.
a kohen reads first. Because he is to be honored for his holiness (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:2).
and it is a widespread custom today. A common custom.

that even an ignorant kohen, etc.. They became accustomed to take only lineage into account, and not the person's own merit, although by law precedence due to lineage applies only if they are equal in Torah knowledge (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 3:2; Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 5:8).
and anyone who is greater than his fellow in wisdom reads first. Out of respect for the Torah.
and the last one who rolls up the Torah scroll. The last person called up, who finishes the reading and afterwards rolls up the scroll (above 5).
receives a reward equal to all of them. Since he completes the Torah reading.
even the greatest in the congregation. Because it is an important reading.
an Israelite goes up. For this cancels the order of precedence.
and no Levite may go up after him at all. So that people not mistakenly regard the first as a kohen.

lest they say the first was disqualified. That he is not a kohen, and they will say that this is why another kohen was called up after him, and therefore the kohen who went up first goes up also in place of the Levite.
what is the order of the Torah reading with the prayer. The manner of combining them.
it became customary to say Kaddish before the maftir goes up. After the required number of readers has been called up (see above 17).
after the prayer leader finishes Tehillah LeDavid and Seder HaYom. Which are said on every Shabbat and festival at the Minchah prayer (above 9:13).
in Chumashim. A Torah scroll divided into separate scrolls, each of the five books by itself.

they do not read from Chumashim... out of respect for the congregation. Because it is not respectful to the congregation to read from a book that lacks the sanctity of a Torah scroll (see Hilchot Sefer Torah 7:14, 10:1).
and they do not roll a Torah scroll in public. From one place in the scroll to another place far from it.
so that he does not burden them, etc.. That they would be forced to wait.
if they needed to read two subjects. For example, on Rosh Chodesh that falls on Shabbat (below 13:4).
one who rolls a Torah scroll. From one place to another.
rolls it from the outside. While standing at the side of the scroll.
and when he binds it. Closes the scroll at the end of the reading or the rolling.
he binds it from the inside. While standing facing the written part.
to stand it on the seam. When it is closed, the seam is in the middle between the two rollers.
the congregation may not leave, etc.. Out of respect for the scroll.

that they complete the Torah in one year. That every year they finish reading the whole Torah in public.
in the portion Bereshit. The portion Bereshit, the beginning of the Torah.

they take out two scrolls on Shabbat morning. And likewise whenever they read the Torah on two subjects (above 12:23).
the one who completes. The last of the seven called up.

an ox or a sheep. This is the portion of the festivals.

and they read as the haftarah: And David spoke. A song about God's help in saving from enemies.
every firstborn. And it mentions the commandments of the pilgrimage festivals.
and they read as the haftarah: Still today at Nob to stand. Dealing with the victory over Israel's enemies and the future redemption.
on Shavuot. On the festival of Shavuot.
seven weeks. The continuation of the portion "Every firstborn" (above 8).
in the third month. Which deals with the giving of the Torah, which occurred on that day.

and this is the blessing. The last portion in the Torah, and on this day they complete the annual cycle of Torah reading (see above 1).
and Solomon stood. Solomon's address at the dedication of the Temple.
after the death of Moses. The beginning of the Book of Joshua, as a continuation of the end of the Torah.
on the offerings of the festival. For each day of Sukkot has a different offering.

these subjects that we have mentioned. Above, halachot 8-12, which are the main reading of that day.
the offering of that day mentioned in the Book of Numbers. The additional offerings special to that festival, written in the portion Pinchas in the Book of Numbers (chapters 28-29).
two scrolls or three. For the cases of taking out three scrolls see below, halachot 23-24.

the dry bones. The story of the dead whom Ezekiel revived, as a sign to all Israel not to despair of the redemption.

from the Priestly Blessing. Because the revolt against the Greeks, which ended in victory and the rededication of the altar, was led by the Hasmoneans, who were priests.

the lamps of Solomon. There it relates the making of all the Temple vessels, including the lamps (I Kings chapter 7).

Comfort, comfort My people. For after the destruction there is a need for comfort.
until Rosh Hashanah. These are seven Shabbatot called the "seven of consolation" (see Seder HaTefillot, 65).

on the portion Shekalim. Which deals with the commandment to give the half-shekel (Exodus 30:11-16), for at that time they would announce that shekels must be brought as a contribution for the public offerings (see Hilchot Shekalim 1:9).
with Jehoiada the priest. It relates there the collection of money for repairing and strengthening the Temple.
during the week. If Rosh Chodesh falls on one of the weekdays of the following week.
on the portion Zachor. Which deals with the commandment to remember what Amalek did and to blot out his memory from the world (Deuteronomy 25:17-19; and see above 17).

the red heifer. The passage dealing with the commandment to prepare ashes from a red heifer, by means of which a person and vessels can be purified from the impurity of the dead (Numbers chapter 19). and I will sprinkle clean water upon you. A prophecy of the ingathering of the exiles and of Israel's purification from impurity.
the one adjacent to the fourth. The one before the Shabbat on which "This month" is read.

in the first month on the first day of the month. It speaks there of the dedication of the Temple on Rosh Chodesh Nisan, and of the festival of Pesach.

for sometimes there will be a break, etc.. Since each of them depends on a different date: the first is before Rosh Chodesh Adar, the second before Purim, and the third two Shabbatot before Rosh Chodesh Nisan.

one reads it from the second scroll. And it is not divided among several readers.

falls in the middle of the week. If it falls on a weekday.
the whole Torah in each year. Every year, according to the accepted and widespread custom (above 1).
to read for himself. To read individually.

and a verse that has no translation. For example, a verse containing only names, or one that is not translated in public (see above 12:12).
to complete his portions with the congregation. That he too will finish a full cycle of Torah reading, together with the congregation's completion.
they lift their hands. They raise their hands and bless the people (the text of the blessing is below in the commentary to 3).

on a fast day. On which there is no concern about drunkenness, since people do not eat on it.
in what case does this apply. That even on a fast they do not lift their hands at Minchah.
and a public fast. Special fasts decreed on the community because of drought or other troubles (see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 4:18).
since their Minchah prayer is close to sunset. This time is later than the time at which they are accustomed to pray Minchah ketanah (see above 3:4).

and went up to the platform. A raised place on which the priests stand when they bless.

are uprooted. Move.
their faces toward the sanctuary. Toward the ark, which is at the front of the synagogue (above 11:2).

say to them. From here they learned that the blessing must be read out to the priests, and that they should not say it on their own.
the first verse. Which is "May the Lord bless you and keep you."

and from the enactments of Rabban Yochanan. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who instituted various enactments after the destruction of the Temple (see also Hilchot Lulav 7:15).

begins to bless on his own. Without the call "Kohanim."

from the world to the world. In both worlds, this world and the World to Come.
